name: cloacal malformation
aliases: urogenital sinus and anorectal malformation complex

clinicalPearls: A cloacal malformation is the most complex anorectal malformation in females, in which the rectum, vagina and urinary tract fail to separate and converge into a single common channel opening as a solitary perineal orifice
The single perineal opening is the clinical hallmark; a female neonate with an imperforate anus and only one perineal opening has a cloaca until proven otherwise

The length of the common channel is the key prognostic and operative determinant, with shorter channels generally more amenable to reconstruction and carrying better continence potential than longer, more complex channels
Associated hydrocolpos (a distended, obstructed vagina) is common and can compress the trigone to cause ureteric obstruction and can become infected, so it must be actively sought and drained
The malformation is frequently part of the VACTERL spectrum, mandating systematic screening for vertebral, cardiac, tracheo-oesophageal, renal and limb anomalies
Sacral and spinal cord anomalies, including a tethered cord and an abnormal sacral ratio, are common and strongly influence future urinary and faecal continence

Initial management is a diverting colostomy with drainage of any hydrocolpos, deferring definitive single-stage reconstruction (such as posterior sagittal anorectovaginourethroplasty, often with total urogenital mobilisation) to a specialist centre

Lifelong multidisciplinary follow-up is required for bowel and bladder function, sexual and reproductive health, and menstrual outflow, as obstructed or duplicated Mullerian structures may present at puberty
reference.pathophysiology: A cloacal malformation arises from failure of normal partitioning of the embryonic cloaca, the common terminal chamber into which the hindgut and urogenital sinus drain. In normal development the urorectal septum descends to divide this chamber into an anterior urogenital sinus and a posterior anorectal canal, while the cloacal membrane breaks down to create separate perineal openings. When this septation and descent are disturbed, the urinary tract, genital tract and rectum remain confluent and drain through a single common channel that opens onto the perineum. The length of this common channel reflects how early and how severely development was disrupted, and associated maldevelopment commonly affects the sacrum, spinal cord, kidneys and Mullerian structures, producing the frequently duplicated or obstructed vagina and uterus and the renal and neurological anomalies that accompany the malformation.
additionalDifferentials: Other anorectal malformations such as rectovestibular or rectoperineal fistula
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia with virilisation and a urogenital sinus
Vaginal atresia or transverse vaginal septum with hydrocolpos
Persistent cloaca as part of caudal regression / sirenomelia spectrum
additionalInvestigations: Examination of the perineum documenting a single opening, with early cloacagram / genitogram and endoscopy (cloacoscopy) to define the common channel and anatomy
Renal and pelvic ultrasound to assess kidneys, hydronephrosis and hydrocolpos
Contrast studies and high-resolution pelvic MRI to map the rectum, vagina, urethra and any Mullerian duplication
Spinal ultrasound or MRI for tethered cord and other cord anomalies
Sacral radiographs to calculate the sacral ratio as a continence predictor
Echocardiography and oesophageal / airway assessment as part of VACTERL screening
Serial renal function and urinary tract imaging, with urodynamic studies during follow-up
redFlags: A female neonate with imperforate anus and a single perineal opening, indicating a cloaca requiring urgent specialist referral
Large or infected hydrocolpos causing ureteric obstruction, abdominal mass or sepsis
Signs of urinary tract obstruction, obstructive uropathy or deteriorating renal function
Features of a serious associated anomaly such as duct-dependent cardiac disease or oesophageal atresia
Abdominal distension or failure to pass meconium indicating bowel obstruction before diversion
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends heavily on the length of the common channel, the quality of the sacrum and spinal cord, and associated renal anomalies; children with short channels and good sacral anatomy often achieve satisfactory urinary and faecal continence, whereas long common channels are associated with greater need for intermittent catheterisation, bowel management and reconstructive interventions. Preservation of renal function and attention to future menstrual, sexual and reproductive function are central long-term goals.
pitfalls: Mislabelling a cloaca as a simple imperforate anus and failing to recognise the single perineal opening
Overlooking hydrocolpos, allowing ureteric obstruction, infection or an enlarging pelvic mass to develop
Neglecting to screen for VACTERL, spinal and renal anomalies that alter management and prognosis
Attempting definitive reconstruction outside an experienced specialist centre without fully delineating the anatomy
Failing to plan for menstrual outflow and Mullerian anomalies, which may present with obstruction at puberty
references: Pena and Bischoff, Surgical Treatment of Colorectal Problems in Children
management: Neonatal diverting colostomy to relieve obstruction, with drainage of any hydrocolpos and decompression of the obstructed urinary tract.
Definitive reconstruction by posterior sagittal anorectoplasty with total urogenital mobilisation or urogenital separation, with the approach tailored to the length of the common channel.
Systematic VACTERL screening and management of associated vertebral, cardiac, tracheo-oesophageal, renal and limb anomalies.
Neurosurgical assessment and release of a tethered cord where present.
Long-term bowel-management programme and clean intermittent catheterisation to optimise faecal and urinary continence.
Renal surveillance to protect upper-tract function, with treatment of vesicoureteric reflux or obstruction.
Multidisciplinary paediatric surgical, urological and gynaecological care, including management of Mullerian duplication and menstrual outflow at adolescence.
